Choose a *Service*: bread (every village), a doctor (towns) or a hospital (the city). The hexagons are its market areas, one for each place that offers it, and the note on the right explains their size. A place that offers a service also offers all the more common ones.

{{< geores sim="central-places" presets="service" >}}
:::

## What to look for

- Choose a doctor: how many villages surround each town? Between how many towns is each of these villages shared?
- Switch from bread to a doctor, then to a hospital: how many times larger does the market area get at each level?
- Are the towns further apart than the villages? And the cities?
- Why does a hospital need a much larger market area than a bakery?
- Why are the market areas hexagons, and not circles?

## How it works

On an even plain, people get each service at the nearest place that offers it. The places sit on a triangular grid: every place is a village, every third place is also a town, every ninth also a city. Each level serves the area closer to it than to any other place of the same level: these areas are hexagons, which cover the plain without gaps or overlaps. Under the market principle (k = 3), the market area of each level is three times that of the level below: a town serves itself and a third of each of its six neighbouring villages.

## Sources

Schematic model after Christaller (1933), the market principle; no data.
